# Goals of the lab overall

The skills acquired in this lab class are crucial for bioinformatic tasks using molecular data, such as data analysis, scripting,
and working in high-performance computing (HPC) environments. My hope is that you don’t just type the commands into the terminal and
move on -- I would like you to ***think*** about what these commands are doing and start imagining how they could be useful in analyzing your own data.

## For your success in the lab
Each lab is inteded to be a reference point for you on various bioinformatic tasks.
To make the most of these labs, please treat them like a **personal resource**, so
adjust any specific commands accordingly.

# Lab Deep-dive

---

### Overview of today's lab
Today's lab will include preparing data for transcript quantification with the
pseudo-alignment tool, [Salmon](https://combine-lab.github.io/salmon/getting-started/introduction/).

This work largely includes uploading and downloading data to and from the W&M's HPC.
The transcriptome and genome are already prepared for you, along with the list of
"decoys" (genome sequence names), which Salmon requires.

As in prior guided-labs, this lab will walkthrough the quantification using
***only one*** of the sequencing runs. You will need to repeat this for all of them.

It is important to acknowledge that there are existing tools/workflows that do
automate many of these steps for you, such as the fantastic NextFlow-Core's
[RNA-seq workflow](https://github.com/nf-core/rnaseq). While this emphasizes
reproducibility, the greatest aim in this lab course is to build your comfort
interacting with the HPC and handling files. This is where repetition is really
powerful, as it really is **practice, practice, practice**!

Make sure to ask questions as needed!

### Moving files, `Salmon`, Transcript Abundance!
- [ ] Logging on to the HPC!
- [ ] Uploading files to the HPC

## Preparing today's lab
Today, we will be using previously published *Drosophila melanogaster* genome and
transcriptome, which were taken from NCBI's RefSeq database, along with a file
containing the names of the genome sequences (these will be Salmon's "decoys").

This will include uploading files to the HPC and doing a little bit of file
manipulation to prepare everything.

1. Download the files for today from Blackboard
   - `Drosophila.Genome.fasta`
   - `Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta`
   - `Drosophila.decoys.txt`

2. Open **two** terminal windows.

3. In **one** of those terminals, log onto the HPC

4. On the HPC and in your lab folder in `scr10`, you should (hopefully) have a
`transcript_quantification` folder. If you do not, then make one
**in your lab folder**

5. Move into the `transcript_quantification` folder
   ```bash
   YOUR CODE HERE
   ```

6. Use `pwd` to view the `PATH` to this folder. Make sure to copy this path!

7. You will use your **local** terminal (not connected to the HPC) to upload data
to the `transcript_quantification`.
   ```bash
   scp [DRAG-FILE-TO-TERMINAL] wm-username@bora.sciclone.wm.edu:[PASTE-THE-PWD-PATH]
   ```

   `scp` works by moving files **from** a location **to** another location.

   By putting the files from your computer first, `scp` will copy those files **from**
   your computer **to** the HPC. Later, we will do the reverse.

8. Once your **local** terminal says the files have uploaded, you can close it.

9. In the remote (HPC) terminal, check that the files are there.

   ::: {.callout-tip title="In case you get stumped" collapse="true"}
   Use the `ls` command to view everything in your folder!
   ```bash
   ls
   ```
   :::

   You should see all three files there!

10. Make a new folder for `Salmon`'s outputs, `Salmon_Quant`

    ::: {.callout-tip title="In case you get stumped" collapse="true"}
    Use the `mkdir` command to make a new folder!
    ```bash
    mkdir Salmon_Quant
    ```
    :::

## Preparing the `Salmon` index

`Salmon` is a pseudo-alignment tool, which quickly "aligns" your raw reads to
a transcriptome. To do make this fast and accurate, `Salmon` needs the transcriptome
formatted in a specific way to facilitate its work. This is called `indexing` and
is a common step for many bioinformatic tools.

1. To generate the indexed dataset for `Salmon`, we need to prepare a file with
the transcriptome **and** genome together since we are using the genome as a "decoy"
to improve the mRNA quantification. This is easily done with another wonderful
terminal command, `cat`.

   `cat` can either show you everything inside a file or "concatenate" (merge)
   files together. Today we will merge the genome and transcriptome.

   ::: {.callout-tip title="How `cat` works"}
   `cat` merges files together in the order that you provide them. This means that
   every subsequent file is "merged" to the bottom of the prior file(s).

   This is really important as `Salmon` expects the genome (our "decoy") sequences
   to be at the bottom of the file. So you just put the transcriptome first followed by
   the genome and make sure to store the output, using `>` to a new file.

   The command is below to help illustrate this! While we are using just two files,
   this command will work for any number of files!

   ```bash
   cat Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta Drosophila.Genome.fasta > Drosophila.Txm_Gnm.fasta
   ```
   :::

2. You can now remove the `Drosophila.Transcriptome.fasta` and `Drosophila.Genome.fasta`
files from the HPC.

   ::: {.callout-tip title="In case you get stumped" collapse="true"}
   ```bash
   rm some-file
   ```
   :::

3. Now we can prepare to generate the `Salmon` index. First, load `conda` and
activate the `txpt_quant` container.

   If you do not have the `txpt_quant` container, refer back to the
   `access-setup-hpc` guided lab on how to make new containers and install software.

4. With your container active, you need to make another job submission script! Go
ahead and copy the `fastq_trim.sh` script and save it as `salmon_run.sh`.

5. Inside this script, you will need to remove the exising `fastp` command, then add
the following commands to generate the `index` that `Salmon` needs for our *Drosophila*
data.
   ```bash
   salmon index \
        -p 8 \
        -d Drosophila.decoys.txt \
        -i dmel_index \
        -t Drosophila.Txm_Gnm.fasta
   ```

    Here is a breakdown of the command:
    - `index`: tells `Salmon` that we are preparing its index
    - `-p`: number of threads to use (this should ideally be the same as `--ntasks`)
    - `-d`: PATH to the `decoys.txt` file (these are just the name of the genome sequences)
    - `-i`: what you would like `Salmon` to name your index
    - `-t`: PATH to the merge transcriptome and genome fasta files

6. All you need to do now is submit the job submission script!

   ::: {.callout-tip title="In case you get stumped" collapse="true"}
   ```bash
   sbatch salmon_run.sh
   ```
   :::

---

## Quantify Transcript Abundance!

With the index prepared, it is fairly easy to start quantifying transcript abundance
from **each** of the trimmed reads, which were prepared before.

1. First, let's update the existing `salmon_run.sh` file. This time instead of
deleting the command, let's leave it there. However, add one `#` in front of each
line in the command to "comment out" the command. This will prevent it from being
run each time this script is submitted.

   This is a nice way to leave useful bits of code in these job submission scripts
   that we use rarely. It can serve as a nice reference for later!

2. Now add the command to run the quantification to the `salmon_run.sh` script.
   ```bash
   salmon quant -i dmel_index \
      -l A \
      -1 forward.fastq.gz \
      -2 reverse.fastq.gz \
      -p 8 \
      -o Salmon_Quant/outname_Quant
   ```

   Here is a breakdown of the command:
   - `quant`: tells `Salmon` that we are quantifying transcript expression
   - `-i`: PATH to the `Salmon` index
   - `-l`: specify what type of sequencing library we used (`A` tells `Salmon` to determine this automatically)
   - `-1`: PATH to the `forward` reads
   - `-2`: PATH to the `reverse` reads
   - `-p`: number of threads to use (this should ideally be the same as `--ntasks`)
   - `-o`: what you would like `Salmon` to name the output directories it is going to make

   There are some placeholder names that you can update!

::: {.callout-caution}
The steps below are to show you how to run the transcript quantification with **just one**
set of trimmed reads.

You will need to update the names as appropriate.

This *can* be automated a bit more, but I want to stress that being pushed to touch
and update these files repeatedly will help it become more familiar and easy to do!
:::

3. For each of the sets of reads, it would be best to provide the **full** path to
the trimmed reads in the script. Especially, as you should be working in your
`transcript_quantification` folder, we do not have to any confusing navigation.

   In the code below are the `PATH`s to ***my*** files. You should update it accordingly!
   ```bash
   salmon quant \
        -i dmel_index \
        -l A \
        -1 /sciclone/scr10/xxmaureralcala/Biol404L/raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Fwd.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
        -2 /sciclone/scr10/xxmaureralcala/Biol404L/raw_read_prep/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1.Rev.20q.80nt.fastq.gz \
        -p 8 \
        -o Salmon_Quant/Dmel_Maine_21C_Rep1_Quant
   ```

   You can see that I added the sample information to the `-o` to make it clear
   which set of trimmed reads were being processed.

4. Submit the `salmon_run.sh` script and feel free to update it with new sets of
reads and repeat!

5. Sit back and rest for a moment! We are finally about to touch some results! Yay!

## Downloading the `Salmon` quantification files

We will be using R-Studio for a brief moment, before downloading the output
transcript-level quantification files from `Salmon`

1. With R-Studio open, go to the `File` menu and select `New Project`

2. In the pop-up menu select `New Directory`

3. Then choose `New Project` and name the new directory `Guided_DGE_Analysis`

4. When prompted, use the menu to put this project as a `sub-directory` of your
`Desltop`

5. You should see the `Guided_DGE_Analysis` on your `Desktop`

6. Inside that folder, make the following new folders
   - [ ] `quant_data`
   - [ ] `metadata`
   - [ ] `results`

7. Open a new **local** terminal and move into `quant_data` folder inside the `Guided_DGE_Analysis` folder

   ::: {.callout-tip title="In case you get stumped" collapse="true"}
   ```bash
   cd [PATH-TO-DRAG-QUANT-DATA-FOLDER]
   ```
   :::

8. Once inside your `quant_data`, we can download ALL of the `Salmon` outputs.
Each sample will be in its own folder. To make it easy, get the `PATH`, using `pwd`,
to the `Salmon_Quant` folder on the HPC.

   **Make sure you are in the `quant_data` folder before continuing!

   When ready, we will use `scp` to download the data **from** the HPC **to** our
   `quant_data` folder locally.

   In your **local** terminal, use `scp` to download the data.

   ```bash
   scp -r wm-username@bora.sciclone.wm.edu:[PATH-TO-SALMON-QUANT-DATA-FOLDER]/Dmel* .
   ```

   ::: {.callout-tip title="For Mac Users" collapse="true"}
   Sometimes the terminal hates the `wildcard` character, `*`. To force it to use
   it in a way that makes sense, you just need to slightly adjust the `scp` command
   ```bash
   scp -r wm-username@bora.sciclone.wm.edu:[PATH-TO-SALMON-QUANT-DATA-FOLDER]/Dmel\* .
   ```
   :::
